records.place: The Bay of Fires winery at Pipers River, north east Tasmania

wine.name: Grand Vintage
wine.grapes: Chardonnay, about two thirds in the releases read, with Pinot Noir for the rest.
wine.sites: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir drawn from vineyards across the island's cool districts and woven into one blend, the idea behind the house's name, a word for tapestry.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method, with the second fermentation in the bottle, then held on its lees, the house's tirage, for years before disgorging: about six years for the 2016, nearly seven for the 2017 and nine for the 2009 by the house's own pages. The dosage is kept low.
wine.glass: Grapefruit, lemon curd and oyster shell over brioche, roasted almond and nougat from the long lees ageing; a fine bead, rich yet taut, with crisp acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink after its long tirage; it can be kept some years more, the toast deepening as the citrus recedes.
wine.serve: 9 to 12 degrees Celsius, as for a fuller, long aged sparkling wine; no decanting; a tulip shaped white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: The house's vintage cuvée: every grape grown in the one year printed on the label.
The island's one Geographical Indication, which covers the whole state.

records.table: House of Arras, founded in 1995, is Tasmania's house of long aged sparkling wine, and Grand Vintage is its vintage cuvée: Chardonnay led, with Pinot Noir, held six years and more on its lees. Grapefruit, oyster shell and brioche give it the weight for a main course.
records.story: The house grew from a search that a winemaker of the Hardy wine company began in 1988 for an Australian home for traditional method sparkling wine, and that search led to Tasmania's cool, maritime north. In 1995 BRL Hardy set up a new venture within the company to make sparkling wine from the island alone, and an internal think tank gave it the name Arras, a word for an intricate, rich tapestry: the house's way of saying that its wines are woven from many Tasmanian sites. The first Grand Vintage, of the 1995 harvest, reached the market at the end of the decade after years on its lees, and long tirage became the mark of the house. Above it the house later added a late disgorged release, held on its lees for a decade and more. The label passed with its parent from the Hardy wine company through the Accolade group, and in 2023 Accolade sold House of Arras, with the Bay of Fires winery and cellar door at Pipers River, to the family owned Handpicked Wines. To a sommelier the Grand Vintage is the bottle that shows what years on the lees do to Tasmania's high natural acidity.

others.name: The late disgorged release
others.note: Held on its lees for a decade and more before disgorging; the house's long aged cuvée above the Grand Vintage.

others.name: Blanc de Blancs
others.note: The house's vintage sparkling wine from Chardonnay alone.

traps: House of Arras is a Tasmanian house founded in 1995, not a Champagne house: the name is a word for tapestry, not the French town.
Australia sets no minimum time on lees comparable to Champagne's; the long tirage of the Grand Vintage is the house's choice, not a rule.

cards.front: House of Arras: what does the word Arras stand for in the house's name?
cards.back: A rich, intricate tapestry: its wines are woven from many Tasmanian sites.

cards.front: Which Tasmanian house sold its business, with the Bay of Fires winery, to Handpicked Wines in 2023?
cards.back: House of Arras, sold by Accolade.

questions.q: A guest asks what gives House of Arras Grand Vintage its brioche and nougat. Which answer fits?
opts: Years on its lees in bottle before disgorging
Fermentation in new French oak barrels
A high dosage of sugar at disgorging
Grapes dried on mats before pressing
questions.exp: The house holds the Grand Vintage on its lees for six to nine years by its own pages, which builds brioche and nougat; the dosage is low, not high.

opts: BRL Hardy
Louis Roederer
Moët Hennessy
Hill-Smith Family Vineyards
questions.exp: BRL Hardy set up the venture within the company in 1995; Louis Roederer was the partner behind Jansz at Pipers River, not Arras.

report: The founding of 1995 rests on the house's own page and on Decanter and Wine Companion; one account dates the start to 1994, when Hardys gave the winemaker the brief, so the record keeps 1995 and agrees with the region record.
The first release is 1998 in one account and four years after the 1995 harvest in another, so the story says the end of the decade.
The name as a word for tapestry and the internal think tank rest on two secondary accounts read through search.
The founding winemaker is living and is described, never named; the late disgorged release carries his name, so it is described too.
The years of the Hardy to Constellation to Accolade changes were not read, so only the sale of 2023 carries a year.
The library's trap that Australia sets no minimum lees ageing comparable to Champagne's is carried over unchanged.

wine.name: Jansz Premium Cuvée
wine.grapes: Chardonnay, usually the larger part, with Pinot Noir; the split moves between releases, and some have held a touch of Meunier.
wine.sites: The estate vineyard at Pipers River on rich, free draining basalt soils, first planted in 1975 under the name Heemskerk, with fruit from other Tasmanian vineyards.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method, which the house calls méthode Tasmanoise: a non vintage blend of base wines given its second fermentation in the bottle, then at least eighteen months on its lees before disgorging, as the house states.
wine.glass: Honeysuckle, lemon zest and fresh strawberry over nougat and roasted nuts from the lees; a creamy mousse, bright acidity and a clean, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink on release without cellaring, as the house advises, and at its liveliest while the fruit is fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, well chilled but never below 5; no decanting; a tulip shaped white wine glass.

label.means: The house's non vintage blend of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
Non vintage: base wines of more than one year blended together.
The island's one Geographical Indication, which covers the whole state.

records.table: Jansz Tasmania was born at Pipers River in 1986 of a partnership with Louis Roederer, and Premium Cuvée is its non vintage: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, eighteen months and more on lees, with honeysuckle, lemon zest and a creamy mousse. Pour it with oysters.
records.story: The name looks back to the Dutch navigator Abel Janszoon Tasman (about 1603 to 1659), who reached the island's west coast in November 1642 in his ship the Heemskerck. In 1975 a vineyard was planted at Pipers River in the cool north east and named Heemskerk after that ship. In 1986 the Champagne house Louis Roederer, drawn by a climate like that of north east France and by the free draining basalt soils, went into partnership with Heemskerk Wines and planted Chardonnay and Pinot Noir there for traditional method sparkling wine alone; the wine took the name Jansz, from Tasman's patronymic. Roederer was a founding partner and did not stay. In 1998 the Hill-Smith family, the South Australian family behind Yalumba, bought the brand and the property and built it as Jansz Tasmania, a family owned house devoted to sparkling wine. The house coined its own term, méthode Tasmanoise, for the traditional method made in its island way. The Premium Cuvée, its non vintage, is the bottle by which most guests meet Tasmanian sparkling wine, and it shows the island's high acidity softened by time on the lees.

others.name: Jansz Vintage Cuvée
others.note: The house's vintage sparkling wine of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, held longer on its lees.

others.name: Jansz Premium Rosé
others.note: The non vintage rosé, of Pinot Noir with Chardonnay and Meunier.

others.name: Jansz Late Disgorged Vintage Cuvée
others.note: A vintage wine held on its lees for years before a late disgorging.

traps: Louis Roederer was a founding partner in 1986, not a later owner: the Hill-Smith family bought the house in 1998.
Méthode Tasmanoise is the house's name for the traditional method, second fermentation in bottle, not a different technique.
Heemskerk was the vineyard's first name and Tasman's ship; Jansz comes from Tasman's own patronymic.

cards.front: Jansz Tasmania: which Champagne house was its partner at Pipers River in 1986?
What is méthode Tasmanoise, in one line?
cards.back: Jansz Tasmania's own name for the traditional method, second fermentation in bottle, made in its island way.

questions.q: A guest asks how long Jansz Premium Cuvée rests on its lees before disgorging. What do you say?
opts: At least eighteen months, by the house's account
At least ten years, as a late disgorged wine
No time at all: it is a tank method wine
Exactly thirty six months, as Champagne law demands
questions.exp: The house gives eighteen months of lees contact for the Premium Cuvée; ten years and more belong to late disgorged wines, and Australian law sets no Champagne minimum.

questions.q: In which year did the Hill-Smith family, behind Yalumba, buy the house that became Jansz Tasmania?
questions.exp: The house dates the Hill-Smith purchase to 1998; 1986 is the year of the partnership with Louis Roederer, and 1975 the first planting as Heemskerk.

report: The founding of 1986 and the Hill-Smith purchase of 1998 rest on the house's own story page and Wine Companion; one account gives 1997 for the purchase and one gives 1987 for the partnership, and both are left aside.

The year Roederer left was not found, so the story says only that it did not stay; one account says the brand was bought from Pipers Brook Vineyard, which held it after Roederer, and this rests on one source, so it is left out.

The Companion to Tasmanian History dates a Heemskerk pilot vineyard to 1966 and a first release to 1976; the record keeps the library's 1975 for the Pipers River planting, which several accounts give.
The blend split varies by source and release (about two thirds Chardonnay, sixty to forty, or with three per cent Meunier), so the grapes are given without figures.
Tasman's birth year is uncertain in the sources (1602 or 1603), so the story says about 1603.

records.place: Pipers Brook, by Pipers River, north east Tasmania

wine.name: Pipers Brook Riesling
wine.sites: Close planted estate vineyards of old Riesling vines in the Pipers Brook district, on red volcanic Ferrosol soils, the krasnozem, in a cool maritime climate near Bass Strait.
wine.making: As the house tells it, the pressed juice has a short time on its skins for aroma and texture, then ferments slowly at very low temperatures in stainless steel; the wine is bottled early under screwcap to keep its freshness.
wine.glass: Lime juice, Meyer lemon and green apple over kaffir lime leaf and a chalky, talc like texture; taut and steely, with fine acidity and a long, zesty finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and taut on release, it keeps for five to ten years and beyond by the house's notes.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass with room for its perfume.

label.means: The estate's name and its district in Tasmania's cool north east.
The island's one Geographical Indication, which covers the whole state.

records.table: Pipers Brook Vineyard, planted in 1974 in Tasmania's cool north east, makes its Riesling in the steely manner of Alsace: from old vines on red volcanic soil, fermented cold in steel, all lime, Meyer lemon and chalk with a long, zesty finish.
records.story: Modern Tasmanian wine began in the south, where Moorilla Estate was founded near Hobart in 1958; the north east came later. In 1974, by the house's own account, two brothers planted Pipers Brook Vineyard in the cool, maritime country near Pipers River, close to Bass Strait. They chose their ground for its likeness in soil, aspect and weather to the cool wine regions of France, Champagne and Alsace among them, and set out to show that the island's north could ripen Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Riesling. The estate became a cornerstone of the Tasmanian wine industry, and its Riesling, modelled on the steely, complex Rieslings of Alsace, became the wine many guests first met from it. At the turn of the century the estate changed hands: the Kreglinger company, whose Australian arm moved into wine production with it, took a majority in 2000 or 2001 by the accounts read, and the de Moor family of Launceston has run it since under the name Kreglinger Wine Estates. In 2024 the vineyard marked fifty years. To a sommelier the Riesling is the north east's argument in a glass: lime and chalk, high acidity and no oak.

others.name: Kreglinger Vintage Brut
others.note: The estate's traditional method sparkling wine, sold under the Kreglinger name.

others.name: Pipers Brook Pinot Noir
others.note: The estate's Pinot Noir from its north east vineyards.

traps: Pipers Brook Vineyard and Pipers River are in Tasmania's north east, not in the Tamar Valley proper, though the house describes itself as of the Tamar Valley.
Kreglinger is the name of the estate's owner and its sparkling label; Pipers Brook is the name of the vineyard and its still wines.

cards.front: Pipers Brook Vineyard: on which soil does its Riesling grow?
cards.back: Red volcanic Ferrosol, the krasnozem, in the Pipers Brook district of north east Tasmania.

cards.front: Which Tasmanian estate, planted in 1974, makes a Riesling modelled on Alsace and passed to Kreglinger around 2001?

questions.q: A guest asks how Pipers Brook Riesling is made. Which answer fits the house's own account?
opts: Cold, slow fermentation in steel, bottled early
Fermented and aged a year in new French oak
Left on its skins for weeks as an orange wine
Pressed from grapes frozen hard on the vine
questions.exp: The house ferments the juice slowly at very low temperatures in stainless steel and bottles it early under screwcap; it has only a short time on the skins, never weeks.

questions.q: Which family company took over Pipers Brook Vineyard at the turn of the century?
opts: Kreglinger
Hill-Smith
Accolade
Shaw + Smith
questions.exp: Kreglinger took a majority in 2000 or 2001 and runs the estate as Kreglinger Wine Estates; the Hill-Smith family bought Jansz, not Pipers Brook.

report: Pick in doubt, kept: the estate's still wines are labelled Pipers Brook and its sparkling Kreglinger; the Riesling is the wine the house models on Alsace and the plan's pick, and no source read named another single flagship.
The house dates the planting to 1974; the Companion to Tasmanian History says 1973, so founded keeps the house's own year and the story hedges it as the house's account.
The Kreglinger year is 2000 in one account and 2001 in two others (one says since 2001), with 1997 in a fourth; the story says 2000 or 2001.
The founders are living and are described as two brothers; the founder's doctorate and any argument on paper were not found in the sources read, so the plan's on paper is not told.
The label term Estate Riesling, once used, was seen only on a retailer's page, so it is left out.
The trap on the Tamar Valley rests on Wine Australia's list of informal districts, which names Pipers River and the Tamar Valley apart, against the house's own wording.

records.place: Back Tea Tree Road near Richmond, Coal River Valley, Tasmania

wine.name: Tolpuddle Pinot Noir
wine.sites: The one vineyard, a gently sloping north east facing site rising from Back Tea Tree Road in the cool, dry Coal River Valley, on light silica over sandstone.
wine.making: Hand picked fruit is fermented as whole berries with a share of whole bunches, about half in recent years and some forty per cent in others, in open wooden and stainless steel fermenters, gently plunged; the wine then spends about ten months in French oak, about a third of it new.
wine.glass: Dark cherry and wild strawberry over violet, aniseed, star anise and cracked pepper from the whole bunches; fine, detailed tannin and a long, bright line of acidity.
wine.ageing: Fragrant within a few years of the vintage, it repays cellaring for a decade and more, up to twelve years by the house's notes.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly for its perfume, or not at all; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The single Coal River Valley vineyard that gives every grape in the bottle.
The island's one Geographical Indication, which covers the whole state.

records.table: Tolpuddle Vineyard is a single Coal River Valley site planted in 1988 and named for the Tolpuddle Martyrs, and Tolpuddle Pinot Noir is its red: whole bunches and French oak, dark cherry, violet and star anise over fine, detailed tannin.
records.story: The name looks back to 1834, when six Dorset farm labourers were transported for forming an agricultural union and became known as the Tolpuddle Martyrs. Their leader, George Loveless (1797 to 1874), a ploughman and Wesleyan preacher, reached Van Diemen's Land that year, and by the vineyard's account he served part of his sentence working on a property near Richmond, land that became part of Tolpuddle Vineyard; pardoned, he sailed for England in 1837. The vineyard was planted in 1988 by a small group of growers and winemakers on a gently sloping, north east facing site in the dry Coal River Valley, with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. In 2011 the cousins behind Shaw + Smith, the Adelaide Hills house, bought it, and since then the freshly picked grapes have crossed Bass Strait to be made at their South Australian winery, while the wine keeps the vineyard's name rather than theirs. To a sommelier it is the Coal River Valley's case for Pinot Noir from one site: a cool island grown red with warm, dry valley ripeness.

others.name: Tolpuddle Chardonnay
others.note: The vineyard's other wine, from Chardonnay planted beside the Pinot Noir.

others.name: Loveless Pinot Noir
others.note: A Pinot Noir of the house named for George Loveless, the martyrs' leader.

traps: Tolpuddle is a Tasmanian vineyard whose grapes are made in the Adelaide Hills by Shaw + Smith, but the wine is Tasmanian and carries the Tolpuddle name.
The Tolpuddle Martyrs were Dorset labourers transported in 1834; the vineyard was planted in 1988, not in their day.

cards.front: Tolpuddle Vineyard: for whom is it named, and why Tasmania?
cards.back: The Tolpuddle Martyrs, Dorset labourers transported for forming a union; their leader worked near Richmond, by the house's account.

cards.front: Which Adelaide Hills house bought a Coal River Valley vineyard planted in 1988 in 2011?

A long stay in new American oak
A blend with Syrah from the mainland
Fermentation with the skins of Riesling

Irish rebels of the Young Ireland rising

report: The founders of 1988 are named differently by different accounts (two or three men); one is living and one died in 2019 without a birth year read, so all are described as a small group of growers and winemakers.

The link of George Loveless to the vineyard's land is the house's claim and is hedged; the ADB says he was assigned to the Lieutenant Governor's farm, so the two accounts may not agree and the integrator may prefer to cut it.
Loveless's death date differs between sources (May, December or January of 1874), but the year 1874 agrees.
The making at Shaw + Smith's South Australian winery rests on two secondary accounts read through search.
The whole bunch share and the oak (about ten months, a third new) are from the house's 2024 and 2025 pages; 2017 was forty per cent whole bunch and thirty per cent new oak.

records.place: Campania, Coal River Valley, southern Tasmania

wine.name: Domaine A Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with small parts of Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Petit Verdot in the vintages read.
wine.sites: The estate's own Stoney Vineyard at Campania, first planted in 1973, in the dry Coal River Valley north of Hobart.
wine.making: Matured in French oak barrels in a temperature controlled cellar for up to three years, then bottled at the winery and aged there for up to a decade before release, as the house tells it; the 2014 was released at eleven years old.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackberry and cedar over tobacco leaf, clove and brick dust; firm, fine tannin and fresh, cool climate acidity, more savoury than sweet.
wine.ageing: Released with years of bottle age and open on release, it lasts for decades; vintages of the early 1990s were judged about half way through their lives.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant an older bottle gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate's first label, above its Stoney Vineyard wines.
The island's one Geographical Indication, which covers the whole state.

records.table: Domaine A, a Coal River Valley estate founded in 1989, makes its Cabernet Sauvignon in the Bordeaux mould: up to three years in French oak and years more in bottle before release, cassis, cedar and tobacco over firm, fine tannin. Decant an older bottle.
records.story: The Stoney Vineyard at Campania, north of Hobart, was first planted in 1973 by a local couple, early in the modern wine history of the Coal River Valley. In 1989 a Swiss couple bought it and founded Domaine A there, with the aim of making wines inspired by Bordeaux on a cool island in the Southern Ocean; the dry, warm valley gave them a chance of ripening Cabernet Sauvignon. They kept the Stoney Vineyard name for a second label and gave the Domaine A label to the wines they judged built for long life. Their method was patience: up to three years in French oak, then up to a decade in bottle at the winery before release, so that the wine reached the market with its tannin already settled. The estate came to be known as one of the island's idiosyncratic houses, its Cabernet more European in its acid and structure than most of Australia's. In 2018, looking to retire, the couple sold Domaine A to the owners of Moorilla Estate, near Hobart, whose winemaker worked alongside the founder on the handover. To a sommelier the Cabernet is Tasmania's case for Bordeaux grapes: savoury, firm and released old.

others.name: Stoney Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The second label, from the same vineyard, made to be approachable sooner.

others.name: Stoney Vineyard Pinot Noir
others.note: The estate's Pinot Noir under its second label.

traps: Domaine A is a Tasmanian estate in the Coal River Valley, not a French domaine; Domaine de l'A is a different estate in Castillon, Bordeaux.
Stoney Vineyard is both the estate's vineyard and its second label; the Domaine A label is the first wine.
The Domaine A Cabernet is released with many years of bottle age, so an older vintage on a list is the house's habit, not a cellar find.

cards.front: Domaine A: how long does its Cabernet Sauvignon wait before release?
cards.back: Up to three years in French oak and up to a decade in bottle at the winery, by the house's account.

cards.front: Which Coal River Valley estate did a Swiss couple found on the Stoney Vineyard in 1989?

questions.q: A guest is surprised that Domaine A Cabernet Sauvignon on the list is over ten years old. What explains it?
opts: The house ages it for years in barrel and bottle before release
The restaurant bought the whole vintage at the estate's closing
Tasmanian law demands ten years of ageing for red wine
The wine is a late disgorged sparkling Cabernet
questions.exp: By its own account the house holds the wine up to three years in French oak and up to a decade in bottle; no Tasmanian law sets any ageing.

questions.q: In which year was Domaine A sold by its Swiss founders to the owners of Moorilla Estate?
questions.exp: The founders sold in 2018 on retiring; 1989 is the year they bought the Stoney Vineyard, and 1973 its first planting.

report: The planting of 1973, the purchase of 1989 and the sale of 2018 rest on the house's own story page with Legend Australia and The Examiner; the buyer of 2018 is living and is described through Moorilla Estate, never named.
The founder died after an accident in Switzerland, aged 79, by The Examiner, but no birth year was read, so the founding couple are described, not named; his wife may be living.

The first planters of 1973 are described as a local couple for want of their dates; the claim of the valley's first commercial vineyard rests on one source, and the oldest on another, so neither is told.

The blend (about ninety per cent Cabernet Sauvignon in 2006 by a retailer's note, with Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Petit Verdot) is given without figures; the 2018 Stoney Vineyard sheet shows the same four grapes.
The proportion of new oak for the first wine was not found; the 2018 Stoney Vineyard notes say new oak was historically not used there, so new oak is not claimed.
The vineyard's aspect (north west facing, or northerly, in one review) rests on one source and is left out.
